# Diagnosing an Opel Corsa-C Blower Fan Failure

When a ventilation fan in a vehicle like the 2006 Opel Corsa-C suddenly cuts out mid-operation, it is often a classic case of an overload protection trigger rather than immediate component death. You described a specific sequence: the fan was running at maximum speed when you turned the ignition on, and after roughly two seconds, it stopped completely. Since you have already verified the fuse box and found no blown fuses, we can eliminate a simple open circuit in the power supply line. The behavior suggests the system detected an anomaly and severed the connection to protect the electrical architecture from further damage.

The most probable culprit in this scenario is a failed resistor pack or a shorted blower motor, which causes the Body Control Module (BCM) or the fan control unit to shut down the circuit immediately. In many automotive electrical systems, particularly those using PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) or stepped resistance controls like the Corsa-C, the low-speed resistors are often mounted inline with the motor. If the motor bearings have seized even slightly, or if the internal windings have developed a short to ground, the current draw spikes instantly. This spike triggers an internal thermal fuse within the control unit or causes the external high-current fuse to blow in a "slow-blow" characteristic that takes a moment to react, manifesting as the brief two-second delay you observed.

Before condemning the entire blower motor assembly, you should isolate the fault between the power source and the load. Start by verifying the voltage at the input terminal of the blower motor while someone attempts to switch the fan speeds. If full battery voltage (approx. 12.6V) is present at the motor terminals but the fan does not spin, the issue lies within the motor itself or the inline resistor pack. If there is no voltage, the fault resides in the control logic or wiring harness.

A critical diagnostic step involves inspecting the blower motor's internal brushes and commutator. Over time, carbon buildup can prevent proper electrical contact, leading to intermittent operation that eventually results in a total stall. Additionally, check for physical obstructions. A common pitfall is attempting to diagnose an electronic fault when a small debris item, such as a loose screw or piece of foam from the dashboard trim, has lodged inside the fan housing and jammed the blades.

If the motor tests good but the system still cuts out, the inline resistor pack is the next suspect. These components degrade over time due to heat cycling. When one of the resistors opens up internally, it breaks the circuit for specific speed settings. In some Corsa-C configurations, a failure in the lowest resistance setting can cause an excessive current draw that trips the protection mechanism entirely, disabling all fan speeds until the system resets or is replaced.

Repairing this issue usually involves swapping the blower motor assembly with a known-good unit to rule out internal shorts. If you replace the motor and the problem persists, investigate the Body Control Module inputs. Ensure the wiring harness connectors are not corroded, which is common in older vehicles exposed to humidity or road salt. Corrosion can create high resistance connections that mimic a short circuit behavior under load, causing the BCM to interpret a valid signal as a fault and disconnect power for safety.

Always remember that automotive electrical diagnostics require isolating variables one by one. Swapping components without verifying the input voltage first often leads to replacing good parts unnecessarily. If you find that the resistance pack is integrated into the control unit rather than a separate inline component, replacing the entire HVAC blower control module may be required. This ensures that any internal thermal fuse within the control logic has also been reset or replaced.
